services.summary: A fully managed application platform for deploying stateless containers as request-driven services, event handlers, scheduled jobs, and finite batch workloads without operating servers or Kubernetes clusters.
concepts: A Cloud Run service exposes a stable HTTPS endpoint while every deployment creates an immutable revision containing the image and configuration.
Instances autoscale per revision from incoming requests, events or CPU utilization; minimum instances reduce startup latency and maximum instances protect cost and downstream systems.
Services handle requests, jobs run finite tasks to completion, and worker pools support continuous non-HTTP workloads; choose the resource type before tuning runtime settings.
applicationFit: Use Cloud Run for stateless APIs, web applications, webhooks, event consumers and containerized functions that fit the managed runtime contract.
Use Cloud Run jobs for migrations, scheduled processing and parallel batch work that must finish rather than listen on an HTTP endpoint.
Choose GKE when Kubernetes APIs, operators, custom scheduling or deep cluster control are requirements; choose Compute Engine when the workload needs VM or operating-system control.

architectureFlows.title: Public API with managed data
architectureFlows.note: A regional Cloud Run service terminates managed HTTPS, runs stateless application code and keeps durable state in managed services.

architectureFlows.title: Event-driven processing
architectureFlows.note: Events are buffered outside the container so delivery, retries and back-pressure are independent of instance lifetime.

architectureFlows.title: Private service-to-service API
architectureFlows.note: Each service uses a dedicated identity; the caller presents a Google-signed ID token and the receiver authorizes the invoker role.

security: Separate deployer identity from runtime service identity. Grant the deployer Service Account User only where needed and give each runtime service account the minimum downstream permissions.

Control inbound reachability with ingress settings and IAM. Public reachability and unauthenticated invocation are separate decisions; private service calls should use ID tokens and Cloud Run Invoker.

Store secrets in Secret Manager, restrict Artifact Registry access, use Binary Authorization where provenance is required, and route private egress through Direct VPC egress or an appropriate connector.
operations: Deploy immutable image digests, test tagged revisions without production traffic, then use percentage traffic splitting for canaries and rapid rollback.
Tune concurrency, CPU, memory, request timeout, minimum instances and maximum instances together; also protect Cloud SQL connection pools and other downstream quotas.
Monitor request latency, error rate, container startup latency, instance count, billable instance time, logs and traces by revision so regressions can be tied to a deployment.
watchPoints: A maximum-instance setting applies per revision; during a traffic split, total service instances can exceed the limit configured on one revision.
The writable container filesystem is disposable. Durable state must be externalized, and startup code must tolerate instance replacement and scale-to-zero.
Request-based and instance-based billing have different CPU-allocation behavior; minimum instances, VPC connectors and dependent services can generate cost even when request volume is low.
cost: Primary Cloud Run charges follow allocated vCPU and memory time, requests, and the selected request-based or instance-based billing mode; usage is rounded to 100-millisecond increments.
Minimum instances reduce cold starts but establish baseline compute spend. Higher concurrency can improve resource sharing when the application is concurrency-safe.
Include outbound data transfer, Serverless VPC Access or VPC networking, Artifact Registry, Cloud Build, logging volume, Cloud SQL and other dependent-service charges.
alternatives: Cloud Run — managed stateless containers, HTTPS services, events and jobs with revision-based deployment.
Google Kubernetes Engine — Kubernetes control, operators, complex scheduling, sidecars and portable cluster APIs.
Compute Engine — VM, operating-system, custom networking or specialized host control.
App Engine — opinionated application platform with versions and language/runtime conventions.

comparisons.name: Cloud Run
comparisons.fit: Best fit for stateless containers, APIs, event handlers and jobs with minimal infrastructure ownership.

comparisons.name: Google Kubernetes Engine
comparisons.fit: Choose when Kubernetes primitives and cluster-level customization are part of the requirement.

comparisons.name: Compute Engine
comparisons.fit: Choose when the application requires VM lifecycle, OS access or specialized machine control.

memoryHooks: Service = stable endpoint; revision = immutable deployment snapshot. Traffic moves between revisions, not between mutable containers.
Invoker IAM controls who can call the service; the runtime service account controls what the running container can access.
Exam clue: fastest managed path for a stateless container with scale-to-zero and HTTPS usually points to Cloud Run.

services.summary: A privileged-access control that requires authorized customer approval before Google personnel can access supported customer data, complementing Access Transparency evidence.
concepts: Google personnel submit a cryptographically signed request containing the reason, resource scope, requested time and access duration; an authorized customer approver accepts, dismisses or later invalidates it.
Notifications can be delivered by email or Pub/Sub, while request history and approval actions remain available through the console, API and Cloud Audit Logs.
Access Approval controls Google administrative access to customer data; it does not approve access by the customer's own users, service accounts or applications.
applicationFit: Use it for regulated workloads that require explicit customer control over exceptional Google personnel access.
Pair it with Access Transparency to see actions taken, Assured Workloads for compliance controls and Key Access Justifications when external-key access needs justification.
Do not treat it as PAM for workforce administrators or as a replacement for IAM, organization policy or VPC Service Controls.

architectureFlows.title: Human approval workflow
architectureFlows.note: A Google support or operational need becomes a time-bound request that cannot proceed until an authorized customer approver acts.

architectureFlows.title: Regulated workload control
architectureFlows.note: Access Approval adds customer authorization to the privileged-access path while other controls protect identity, keys and the service perimeter.

security: Grant request-view and request-approval permissions to separate groups where segregation of duties is required; avoid broad project roles for approvers.
Protect Pub/Sub notification subscriptions and approval automation because approval actions are privileged administrative decisions.
Review Access Approval Admin Activity logs and Access Transparency records together; retain evidence according to regulatory requirements.
operations: Configure settings and notification channels at the correct organization, folder or project scope, then test request visibility and escalation ownership.
Track pending, approved, dismissed, expired, policy-approved and invalidated requests; establish an on-call process for time-sensitive requests.
Use Logs Explorer filters for accessapproval.googleapis.com and monitor notification delivery so pending requests do not become silent operational blockers.
watchPoints: Unsupported services or data paths are outside the Access Approval control boundary; confirm service coverage before claiming compliance.
Approving a request authorizes the stated Google personnel access for its scope and duration; it does not prove that access occurred—use Access Transparency for that evidence.
If approvers or notification channels are unavailable, support activity can be delayed; design break-glass governance and escalation deliberately.
cost: Access Approval availability and commercial terms can depend on the support or compliance offering associated with the organization.
Include Pub/Sub, Cloud Logging retention and SIEM export costs used for notifications and evidence.
Operational cost is driven mainly by approval ownership, 24×7 response expectations and audit-evidence handling rather than request throughput.
alternatives: Access Approval — explicit customer consent for Google personnel access.
Access Transparency — records actions Google personnel performed; it does not request customer approval.
Privileged Access Manager — governs time-bound elevated access for customer-managed principals.
Key Access Justifications — provides reasons for externally managed encryption-key access.

comparisons.name: Access Approval
comparisons.fit: Best fit when customer consent must precede supported Google personnel access.

comparisons.name: Access Transparency
comparisons.fit: Choose for visibility and evidence of Google personnel actions.

comparisons.name: Privileged Access Manager
comparisons.fit: Choose for just-in-time elevated access by workforce or workload principals.

memoryHooks: Approval answers “may Google personnel access this data?”; Transparency answers “what did Google personnel do?”
Requests are scoped and time-bound and can be approved, dismissed or invalidated.
Exam clue: explicit customer authorization before Google support access points to Access Approval.

consoleSteps.detail: Grant least-privilege administrative and runtime roles; configure network, encryption and audit controls appropriate to the service.

services.summary: The account, reporting, export, budget and cost-management control plane that links Google Cloud projects to payment responsibility and exposes usage and pricing data for FinOps.
concepts: A Cloud Billing account pays for linked projects and is associated with a Google payments profile; project resource hierarchy and billing-account hierarchy are related but separate.
Reports, cost tables and BigQuery billing export expose cost and usage at different levels of detail; exports should be enabled early because historical detail is not recreated retroactively.
Budgets compare actual and forecast spend with thresholds and notifications, but a budget does not automatically cap consumption unless automation acts on its Pub/Sub notification.
applicationFit: Use Cloud Billing to link projects, assign billing roles, analyze spend, configure budgets and export detailed cost data.
Use BigQuery billing export with labels, tags, folders and projects for allocation, chargeback and unit-cost analysis.
Use quotas, organization policy or controlled automation when spending must be constrained; budget alerts alone are informational.

architectureFlows.title: FinOps reporting pipeline
architectureFlows.note: Detailed billing records flow into an analytics dataset where finance and engineering teams build allocation, anomaly and forecast views.

architectureFlows.title: Budget notification and response
architectureFlows.note: Budgets evaluate scoped spend and publish threshold events; a controlled automation path decides whether to notify, open a ticket or apply an approved action.

security: Separate Billing Account Administrator, User, Viewer and Costs Manager duties; project creation rights should not imply billing administration.
Restrict BigQuery export datasets because they reveal organization-wide consumption, project names, pricing and discount information.
Use audit logs and periodic access reviews for project-billing links, billing account IAM, budgets and export configuration.
operations: Enable billing export when the account is created, validate daily ingestion and monitor schema changes before downstream reports fail.
Define project naming, labels and tags before chargeback; missing allocation metadata cannot be repaired reliably after usage occurs.
Reconcile invoices, cost reports, credits and exports with documented timing differences rather than expecting every surface to match in real time.
watchPoints: Budgets alert; they do not impose a hard spending limit.
Billing export data arrives with latency and can receive corrections; pipelines must tolerate late and adjusted records.
Unlinking or disabling billing can stop billable services in a project and may cause workload disruption.
cost: Cloud Billing tools do not replace the charges from the underlying services represented in reports.
BigQuery storage and query processing, Looker dashboards, Pub/Sub notifications and automation incur their own charges.
Poor partition filtering or repeated full scans of detailed exports can turn cost reporting into a noticeable cost driver.
alternatives: Cloud Billing — authoritative Google Cloud account, invoice, cost and usage management.
Cloud Hub optimization — centralized application and resource recommendations, not the billing ledger.
Recommender — service-specific optimization recommendations, not invoice or payment management.
Cloud Quotas — capacity and rate governance, not financial budgeting.

comparisons.name: Cloud Billing
comparisons.fit: Best fit for payment responsibility, cost reporting, exports and budgets.

comparisons.name: Recommender
comparisons.fit: Choose for actionable service optimization recommendations.

comparisons.name: Cloud Quotas
comparisons.fit: Choose to govern API and resource capacity rather than monetary spend.

memoryHooks: Billing account pays; project consumes. IAM must be managed at both boundaries.
Budget ≠ cap. Use Pub/Sub plus governed automation for actions.
Enable BigQuery export early; detailed historical data is not backfilled.

consoleSteps.detail: Set billing account, project linkage, budgets/alerts and BigQuery billing export.

consoleSteps.detail: Grant least-privilege administrative and runtime roles; configure network, encryption and audit controls appropriate to the service.

consoleSteps.title: Validate operation
consoleSteps.detail: validate cost-table freshness, budget notifications and export queries.

services.summary: An application-centric operations surface that aggregates health, incidents, deployments, security findings, costs and recommendations for Google Cloud resources and App Hub applications.
concepts: Cloud Hub presents centralized data and insights in project views or application views; App Hub supplies the logical application, service and workload model.
Application Design Center can design and deploy resources that become App Hub applications, while existing supported resources can be registered into applications.
Cloud Hub is an aggregation and action surface over operational systems; source services remain authoritative for metrics, findings, incidents, costs and recommendations.
applicationFit: Use Cloud Hub when platform and application teams need one application-centric view across resources and projects.
Use App Hub to group existing resources by business application and expose service/workload ownership before relying on application views.
Continue using specialist products such as Cloud Monitoring, Security Command Center and Cloud Billing for deep investigation and configuration.

architectureFlows.title: Application-centric operations
architectureFlows.note: Resources across projects are registered as App Hub services and workloads, then Cloud Hub correlates operational signals around the application.

architectureFlows.title: Designed application lifecycle
architectureFlows.note: Application Design Center creates an architecture and deployment; Cloud Hub surfaces deployment state, updates and operational posture.

security: Grant Cloud Hub, App Hub and source-service permissions according to operational role; visibility across projects can expose sensitive inventory and findings.
Use management projects and application boundaries deliberately so centralized operators see the intended estate without acquiring broad mutation rights.
Audit registration, application ownership and remediation actions in their source services; Cloud Hub presentation does not replace source audit logs.
operations: Establish application ownership and register supported resources before treating application views as complete.
Validate that required APIs and data providers are enabled in the management project and that operators can follow links into source services.
Use Cloud Hub to prioritize cross-product issues, then verify remediation in the authoritative product and monitor recurrence.
watchPoints: Unsupported or unregistered resources can make an application view incomplete.
Cloud Hub aggregates data; freshness, retention and available actions depend on each source product.
Project views and application views answer different questions—do not infer application ownership solely from project membership.
cost: Cloud Hub itself is primarily a management experience, while monitored resources and connected source services retain their normal pricing.
App Hub/Application Design Center deployments create billable Google Cloud resources.
Logging, monitoring, security, recommendation and analytics retention can dominate the cost of the operational view.
alternatives: Cloud Hub — cross-product application and resource insights with action links.
Cloud Monitoring — deep metrics, dashboards, uptime checks and alerting.
Security Command Center — security posture, findings and threat management.
Cloud Billing — authoritative cost, usage and payment analysis.

comparisons.name: Cloud Hub
comparisons.fit: Best fit for centralized application-centric health and action across products.

comparisons.name: Cloud Monitoring
comparisons.fit: Choose for telemetry, SLOs, dashboards and alert policies.

comparisons.name: Security Command Center
comparisons.fit: Choose for security findings, posture and threat investigation.

memoryHooks: Cloud Hub is the unified view; App Hub supplies the application model.
Application view follows registered services/workloads, not merely a folder or project.
Use Cloud Hub to prioritize, then remediate in the authoritative source service.

services.summary: Google's identity-as-a-service platform for centrally managing workforce users, groups, devices, federation, single sign-on and access context without requiring Google Workspace productivity licenses.
concepts: The Cloud Identity customer/organization contains users, groups, organizational units and devices; managed Google Accounts become principals for Google Cloud and configured SaaS applications.
Federation and directory synchronization connect external identity providers such as Active Directory or Microsoft Entra ID, while Google remains the relying platform for managed accounts.
Cloud Identity manages workforce identity and device posture; IAM grants permissions to Google Cloud resources and Identity Platform serves application customers.
applicationFit: Use Cloud Identity to provision workforce identities, groups and devices for organizations that need Google Cloud access without full Google Workspace.
Use SAML/OIDC SSO, directory synchronization or federation to keep an external directory authoritative and reduce duplicate credential management.
Use Identity Platform for customer sign-in and Workforce Identity Federation when external workforce identities should access Google Cloud without synchronized Google accounts.

architectureFlows.title: Hybrid workforce identity
architectureFlows.note: An enterprise directory remains authoritative while accounts and groups are synchronized or federated into Cloud Identity for Google Cloud and SaaS access.

architectureFlows.title: Context-aware workforce access
architectureFlows.note: User identity and device state contribute to an access decision before the workforce reaches a protected application.

security: Protect super administrator accounts with phishing-resistant MFA, separate daily-use identities and emergency access procedures.
Use groups for role assignment, automate joiner/mover/leaver lifecycle and prevent unmanaged consumer accounts from retaining corporate identity.
Combine device management and context-aware access with IAM least privilege; identity assurance does not itself grant resource permissions.
operations: Define the authoritative directory and immutable identifiers before synchronization; test rename, suspension and deletion behavior.
Monitor provisioning errors, group membership changes, SSO certificate expiry, device compliance and administrator audit events.
Stage federation and SSO changes with break-glass administrators so a configuration error does not lock out the organization.
watchPoints: Cloud Identity, Google Workspace, IAM, Workforce Identity Federation and Identity Platform serve different identity populations and control planes.
Group membership propagation and directory synchronization are not instantaneous; design access-change expectations accordingly.
Deleting or renaming identities can affect resource ownership, audit attribution and application mappings.
cost: Cloud Identity Free and Premium editions provide different device, security and management capabilities; verify edition requirements.
Directory synchronization infrastructure, third-party IdP licensing and endpoint-management operations remain external costs.
Audit export, SIEM retention and context-aware access dependencies can add platform cost.
alternatives: Cloud Identity — managed workforce users, groups, devices and SSO.
Workforce Identity Federation — external workforce access to Google Cloud without synchronizing Google accounts.
Identity Platform — customer identity for applications.
Managed Microsoft AD — managed Windows domain services for domain-joined workloads.

comparisons.name: Cloud Identity
comparisons.fit: Best fit for managed workforce accounts, groups, devices and SaaS SSO.

comparisons.name: Workforce Identity Federation
comparisons.fit: Choose when external workforce identities should access Google Cloud without account synchronization.

comparisons.name: Identity Platform
comparisons.fit: Choose for customer authentication inside an application.

memoryHooks: Cloud Identity manages workforce identities; IAM authorizes those identities to resources.
Identity Platform is CIAM; Managed Microsoft AD is domain service; neither replaces Cloud Identity workforce lifecycle.
Exam clue: central Google-managed users/groups without Workspace productivity apps points to Cloud Identity.

services.summary: A governed procurement and deployment channel for Google, partner and open-source solutions delivered as SaaS subscriptions, VM images, Kubernetes applications and professional services.
concepts: Marketplace listings package commercial terms, deployment metadata, support ownership and billing integration; the deployed software still runs in vendor SaaS or customer Google Cloud resources.
Private Marketplace lets administrators curate products approved for organization, folder or project members, while product requests provide a governed exception path.
Private offers bind negotiated pricing and duration to a Cloud Billing account; infrastructure charges for VM and Kubernetes products remain separate from software pricing.
applicationFit: Use Marketplace to shorten procurement and deploy supported third-party software with consolidated Google Cloud billing.
Use Private Marketplace when platform teams must restrict deployment to security- and procurement-approved products.
Use an internal golden-image or software catalog when the artifact is private, self-supported or not distributed through Marketplace.

architectureFlows.title: Governed product deployment
architectureFlows.note: An administrator curates approved listings; a project user selects a product and deploys it into the permitted Google Cloud environment.

architectureFlows.title: Private-offer procurement
architectureFlows.note: Negotiated commercial terms are accepted against the intended billing account before the entitlement becomes active.

security: Separate procurement, billing-account, Marketplace governance and deployment roles; accepting an offer should require explicit commercial authority.
Review listing permissions, vendor support, data flows, image provenance and required service accounts before approval.
Use organization policies, VPC controls and workload IAM after deployment; Marketplace approval does not make the runtime automatically secure.
operations: Track subscriptions, offer renewal dates, product updates, deployment-manager ownership and vendor support contacts.
Patch or replace Marketplace images and applications according to vendor guidance; listing updates do not necessarily update running deployments.
Test entitlement cancellation and resource deletion separately to avoid either orphaned infrastructure or accidental service interruption.
watchPoints: Private Marketplace scope determines catalog visibility, not permission to create every underlying resource.
Private-offer discounts may exclude Google Cloud infrastructure and can revert or require renewal when the contract ends.
Responsibility is shared among Google, vendor and customer; validate support and SLA boundaries per listing.
cost: Model software subscription or usage charges separately from Compute Engine, GKE, storage, networking and logging charges.
Private offers can change price and commitment term; monitor renewal and post-contract pricing.
Idle deployed infrastructure can continue billing even if the Marketplace subscription changes or is cancelled.
alternatives: Cloud Marketplace — curated commercial software procurement and deployment.
Private internal catalog — organization-owned artifacts and deployment templates.
Artifact Registry — package and container storage, not commercial procurement.

comparisons.name: Cloud Marketplace
comparisons.fit: curated commercial software procurement and deployment.

comparisons.name: Private internal catalog
comparisons.fit: organization-owned artifacts and deployment templates.

comparisons.name: Artifact Registry
comparisons.fit: package and container storage, not commercial procurement.

memoryHooks: Marketplace governs acquisition; IAM and policy still govern the deployed workload.
Private Marketplace curates listings; private offers customize commercial terms.
Exam clue: approved third-party software with consolidated billing points to Cloud Marketplace.

services.summary: A centralized service for observing Google Cloud resource and API quotas, setting quota preferences, creating alerts and requesting or automating supported limit adjustments.
concepts: Allocation quotas limit resources such as CPUs or IP addresses; rate quotas limit operations over time. Quota values can vary by project, region, service and dimension.
A quota preference records the desired limit and can initiate an adjustment request; approval and resulting effective quota depend on service policy and capacity.
Quota adjuster can proactively request increases for supported quotas, while monitoring and alerts expose approaching saturation.
applicationFit: Use Cloud Quotas for inventory, alerting and adjustment workflows across Google Cloud services.
Request increases before launches or migrations and validate regional dimensions, not only the global service total.
Use application rate limiting and capacity controls as well; a larger provider quota does not protect downstream systems or budget.

architectureFlows.title: Capacity readiness workflow
architectureFlows.note: Teams compare forecast demand with current effective quotas, request changes and verify approval before rollout.

architectureFlows.title: Automated quota governance
architectureFlows.note: Monitoring and supported quota adjuster settings reduce surprise exhaustion while keeping human review for capacity and cost risk.

security: Limit quota-administration permissions because increases can expand spend and resource exposure.
Separate quota requesters from budget owners for high-cost capacity and audit preference changes.
Do not put secrets in request justification; use Cloud Audit Logs for administrative review.
operations: Maintain a quota baseline for critical projects and regions and recheck it before major releases.
Alert on both utilization percentage and remaining absolute headroom; low-limit quotas can fail before percentage alerts are useful.
Handle RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED differently from IAM, billing and regional-capacity errors.
watchPoints: A quota increase is not a capacity reservation and does not guarantee zonal or regional stock.
Some quotas are fixed or not supported by the quota adjuster; availability varies by service and project.
Quota dimensions matter: sufficient global quota does not resolve a region-specific limit.
cost: Cloud Quotas has no meaningful standalone workload charge, but approved increases enable billable consumption.
Monitoring, logging and automation used for quota governance can incur charges.
Over-requesting capacity can increase cost risk even when actual billing remains usage-based.
alternatives: Cloud Quotas — provider quota visibility and adjustment.
Cloud Billing budgets — financial thresholds and alerts.
Application rate limiter — protects an API or dependency at runtime.

comparisons.name: Cloud Quotas
comparisons.fit: provider quota visibility and adjustment.

comparisons.name: Cloud Billing budgets
comparisons.fit: financial thresholds and alerts.

comparisons.name: Application rate limiter
comparisons.fit: protects an API or dependency at runtime.

memoryHooks: Quota is a service limit, not a budget and not a reservation.
Preference is desired quota; effective limit is what the service currently enforces.
Exam clue: RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED before a planned launch requires quota review and possibly adjustment.

services.summary: A Kubernetes-native infrastructure controller that represents Google Cloud resources as custom resources and continuously reconciles their desired state through the Kubernetes API.
concepts: Config Connector installs CRDs in the cnrm.cloud.google.com API group; Kubernetes manifests become desired state for supported Google Cloud resources.
Controllers reconcile resource specifications against Google Cloud using the Config Connector IAM identity, not the identity of the person who submitted the manifest.
Namespaces can map to projects and deletion policy determines whether deleting the Kubernetes object deletes or abandons the underlying cloud resource.
applicationFit: Use Config Connector when teams already operate Kubernetes/GitOps and want cloud resources managed through the same declarative API.
Use policy controllers and admission controls to govern manifests before reconciliation.
Prefer Terraform or Infrastructure Manager when Kubernetes is not the desired control plane or plan/review workflows are central.

architectureFlows.title: GitOps cloud-resource lifecycle
architectureFlows.note: A reviewed manifest enters a cluster; Config Connector reconciles it into a Google Cloud resource and publishes status back to Kubernetes.

architectureFlows.title: Policy-controlled platform API
architectureFlows.note: Platform teams expose approved custom resources while admission policy blocks unsafe regions, networks or public exposure.

security: Grant the Config Connector service account only permissions needed by the resource types and projects it reconciles.
Use namespace/project mappings, admission policy and RBAC to prevent manifest authors from indirectly creating privileged cloud resources.
Protect the cluster and GitOps repository because control-plane compromise can mutate the managed Google Cloud estate.
operations: Monitor resource conditions, Kubernetes events, controller health and reconciliation latency; investigate UpdateFailed rather than repeatedly reapplying.
Pin and test Config Connector upgrades because CRD schemas and controllers evolve.
Choose reconcile intervals carefully to balance drift correction against API quota and operational noise.
watchPoints: Deleting a Kubernetes object can delete the cloud resource unless abandon behavior is configured.
Out-of-band cloud changes may be reverted by reconciliation or cause conflicts; establish one authoritative owner.
Some immutable field changes require recreation and some resources or fields have support limitations.
cost: Config Connector itself is open-source/managed tooling, while GKE, cluster operations and created Google Cloud resources are billable.
Frequent reconciliation can contribute to API quota usage and logging volume.
Running a dedicated management cluster adds compute and operational cost.
alternatives: Config Connector — Kubernetes-native cloud resource reconciliation.
Terraform with Infrastructure Manager — plan-based infrastructure deployment.
Crossplane — multi-provider Kubernetes control plane.

comparisons.name: Config Connector
comparisons.fit: Kubernetes-native cloud resource reconciliation.

comparisons.name: Terraform with Infrastructure Manager
comparisons.fit: plan-based infrastructure deployment.

comparisons.name: Crossplane
comparisons.fit: multi-provider Kubernetes control plane.

memoryHooks: The controller identity performs cloud API actions, not the manifest submitter.
Kubernetes object deletion policy determines cloud-resource deletion versus abandonment.
Exam clue: manage Google Cloud resources through Kubernetes CRDs points to Config Connector.

services.summary: The primary command-line interface for authenticating to, configuring and automating Google Cloud services through consistent command groups, named configurations and machine-readable output.
concepts: Named configurations contain properties such as active account, project, region and zone; switching configuration changes client defaults, not server-side resource policy.
gcloud user authentication, application-default credentials and service-account/workload federation credentials serve different consumers and should not be conflated.
Commands expose alpha, beta and generally available surfaces; scripts should pin assumptions, use explicit flags and consume structured output.
applicationFit: Use gcloud for interactive administration, diagnostics, CI/CD steps and repeatable service operations.
Use client libraries when an application needs typed APIs, retries and long-lived integration; use Terraform/Infrastructure Manager for declarative resource lifecycle.
Use Cloud Shell for an immediately authenticated browser environment, while keeping production automation in versioned pipelines.

architectureFlows.title: Operator command flow
architectureFlows.note: A named configuration selects client defaults; credentials obtain a token; the command invokes a Google Cloud API and receives structured output.

architectureFlows.title: CI/CD automation
architectureFlows.note: A workload identity authenticates without a stored service-account key and the script uses explicit project and noninteractive settings.

security: Prefer workforce/workload identity federation or impersonation over downloaded service-account keys.
Use least-privilege identities, verify the active account/project before destructive commands and separate configurations for environments.
Do not expose access tokens, credential files or verbose sensitive output in shell history and CI logs.
operations: Use named configurations, explicit flags and versioned scripts; validate exit codes and parse JSON rather than human table output.
Update components in controlled environments and test scripts against release-channel changes.
Use --verbosity and API audit logs for troubleshooting, but sanitize logs before sharing.
watchPoints: gcloud auth application-default login configures ADC for local applications; it is distinct from gcloud's own active account.
Implicit project/region defaults can target the wrong environment; production automation should specify them explicitly.
Alpha and beta commands can change and may require different components or APIs.
cost: The CLI has no separate per-command charge, but invoked APIs and created resources retain normal pricing.
Cloud Shell quotas and persistent storage differ from local or CI environments.
Verbose logging and automated polling can increase API requests and log volume.
alternatives: gcloud CLI — interactive and scripted Google Cloud administration.
Client libraries — application integration with typed APIs and retry behavior.
Terraform/Infrastructure Manager — declarative infrastructure state and deployment.

comparisons.fit: interactive and scripted Google Cloud administration.

comparisons.name: Client libraries
comparisons.fit: application integration with typed APIs and retry behavior.

comparisons.name: Terraform/Infrastructure Manager
comparisons.fit: declarative infrastructure state and deployment.

memoryHooks: Configuration selects defaults; IAM still decides authorization.
gcloud credentials and ADC credentials are separate contexts.
Exam clue: one-off administration or shell automation usually points to gcloud, not an application SDK.

services.summary: A customer identity and access management service for adding secure sign-up, sign-in, federation, MFA and multi-tenant user isolation to web, mobile and API applications.
concepts: Identity Platform authenticates application users with email/password, phone, social, OIDC and SAML providers and issues tokens that the application backend validates.
A project can use a default user pool or tenants; each tenant isolates users, providers, IAM/auditing configuration, quotas and usage reporting for B2B SaaS boundaries.
Authentication proves user identity; application authorization still belongs in backend policy, claims and data-access rules.
applicationFit: Use Identity Platform for customer or partner authentication when the application should not store passwords or build federation flows.
Use tenants when customers or business units require isolated user stores and identity-provider configuration within one project.
Use Cloud Identity for workforce accounts and Workforce Identity Federation for external workforce access to Google Cloud resources.

architectureFlows.title: Web application sign-in
architectureFlows.note: The client completes a configured sign-in flow, receives an Identity Platform token and presents it to an application backend.

architectureFlows.title: Multi-tenant SaaS identity
architectureFlows.note: The application selects a tenant before sign-in so each customer has isolated users and provider settings.

security: Enforce MFA and strong provider configuration where risk requires it; protect Admin SDK credentials and tenant-management APIs.
Validate token issuer, audience, signature, expiry and tenant context on every backend; never trust client-supplied user IDs.
Use blocking functions and audit logs carefully for account policy, and rate-limit abuse-prone sign-up and password-reset paths.
operations: Monitor sign-in success, provider errors, MAU, SMS delivery, tenant usage and account-abuse indicators.
Plan user migration, password-hash compatibility and account-linking behavior before cutover.
Maintain recovery procedures for provider certificate/secret rotation and administrator lockout.
watchPoints: Identity Platform authenticates customers; it does not grant Google Cloud IAM permissions.
Tenant features and supported controls differ from the non-tenant project and have documented limitations.
Phone/SMS and federation failures can depend on external providers, geography and anti-abuse controls.
cost: Most providers are billed by monthly active users; SAML/OIDC and phone/MFA have distinct pricing dimensions.
SMS messages, Cloud Functions/blocking functions, logging and backend resources add cost.
Anonymous-user cleanup and tenant usage reporting affect cost control.
alternatives: Identity Platform — customer and partner application authentication.
Cloud Identity — managed workforce accounts, groups, devices and SaaS SSO.
Workforce Identity Federation — external workforce access to Google Cloud.

comparisons.name: Identity Platform
comparisons.fit: customer and partner application authentication.

comparisons.name: Cloud Identity
comparisons.fit: managed workforce accounts, groups, devices and SaaS SSO.

comparisons.name: Workforce Identity Federation
comparisons.fit: external workforce access to Google Cloud.

memoryHooks: Identity Platform = CIAM; Cloud Identity = workforce identity.
Tenant isolates users and IdP configuration inside one project.
Authentication token verification comes before application authorization.

consoleSteps.title: Open Identity Platform
consoleSteps.detail: Google Cloud Console → Identity Platform; select the intended scope and supported location.

consoleSteps.title: Configure the service
consoleSteps.detail: Set providers, authorized domains, tenant settings and application credentials.

consoleSteps.title: Apply security boundaries
consoleSteps.detail: Grant least-privilege administrative and runtime roles; configure network, encryption and audit controls appropriate to the service.

consoleSteps.title: Validate operation
consoleSteps.detail: complete sign-up/sign-in, validate token claims and test account protection.

services.summary: A managed Terraform execution and state service that turns versioned blueprints into Google Cloud infrastructure deployments, revisions and pre-apply previews.
concepts: Infrastructure Manager calls Terraform configurations blueprints and creates regional deployments whose revisions represent applied infrastructure state.
A preview executes Terraform plan so proposed create, update, replace and delete actions can be reviewed before deployment.
Blueprint sources can come from local content, Cloud Storage or Git, while a deployment service account performs resource operations.
applicationFit: Use Infra Manager when teams want Google-managed Terraform execution, state and deployment lifecycle on Google Cloud.
Use previews as an approval gate and Cloud Build integration for automated infrastructure delivery.
Use Config Connector for Kubernetes-native reconciliation and Cloud Deploy or application pipelines for application releases.

architectureFlows.title: Reviewed infrastructure deployment
architectureFlows.note: A versioned Terraform blueprint is previewed, approved and applied by a least-privilege deployment identity.

architectureFlows.title: CI infrastructure pipeline
architectureFlows.note: Cloud Build validates the blueprint, creates a preview and promotes the reviewed configuration into an Infra Manager deployment.

security: Use a dedicated deployment service account with only permissions required by the blueprint; separate preview/deployment operators from resource administrators.
Secure Git and Cloud Storage blueprint sources and pin module/provider versions to reduce supply-chain risk.
Review plans for IAM, public exposure and destructive replacement; policy checks should run before deployment.
operations: Track deployment and revision state, preview results, Cloud Build execution and drift caused by out-of-band changes.
Promote immutable blueprint versions through environments rather than editing production deployments ad hoc.
Test deletion and failed-update recovery because managed execution does not remove Terraform lifecycle semantics.
watchPoints: Infra Manager deploys infrastructure, not application binaries or runtime configuration.
A successful preview is a point-in-time plan; source, state or remote resources can change before apply.
Terraform provider/version support and deployment location must be checked before standardizing.
cost: Charges include Infrastructure Manager operation/pricing terms plus resources created by Terraform.
Cloud Build, Cloud Storage artifacts, logging and source hosting can add cost.
Preview frequency and long-running deployments affect operational usage even when no resource change is applied.
alternatives: Infrastructure Manager — managed Terraform previews, state and deployments.
Config Connector — continuous Kubernetes CRD reconciliation.
Terraform in CI — self-managed runners, backend and execution controls.

comparisons.name: Infrastructure Manager
comparisons.fit: managed Terraform previews, state and deployments.

comparisons.name: Config Connector
comparisons.fit: continuous Kubernetes CRD reconciliation.

comparisons.name: Terraform in CI
comparisons.fit: self-managed runners, backend and execution controls.

memoryHooks: Blueprint = Terraform configuration; preview = plan; deployment revision = applied lifecycle state.
Deployment service account owns cloud API actions.
Exam clue: managed Google Cloud Terraform execution with previews points to Infra Manager.

consoleSteps.title: Open Infrastructure Manager
consoleSteps.detail: Google Cloud Console → Infrastructure Manager; select the intended scope and supported location.

consoleSteps.title: Configure the service
consoleSteps.detail: Set deployment location, Terraform source, variables, service account and state behavior.

consoleSteps.title: Apply security boundaries
consoleSteps.detail: Grant least-privilege administrative and runtime roles; configure network, encryption and audit controls appropriate to the service.

consoleSteps.title: Validate operation
consoleSteps.detail: preview/deploy, inspect operation logs and validate update/delete handling.

services.summary: A highly available, hardened Microsoft Active Directory domain service operated by Google for Windows-integrated workloads, domain join, LDAP/Kerberos and forest trust connectivity.
concepts: Managed Microsoft AD runs real Microsoft AD domain controllers while Google handles controller deployment, patching, backup and core service maintenance.
Each selected region receives two domain controllers in non-overlapping zones; adding regions improves locality and domain resilience.
Forest trusts connect a managed resource forest to on-premises or self-managed AD; DNS forwarding and hybrid network connectivity are prerequisites.
applicationFit: Use it for Windows and legacy applications that require AD domain join, Kerberos, LDAP, group policy or SQL Server integration without self-managing controllers.
Use Shared VPC and trusts for multi-project resource-forest patterns connected to an existing identity forest.
Use Cloud Identity for workforce SaaS/Google accounts; it does not provide Windows domain services.

architectureFlows.title: Hybrid resource forest
architectureFlows.note: On-premises identities access domain-joined Google Cloud workloads through private connectivity, DNS forwarding and a forest trust.

architectureFlows.title: Multi-region AD service
architectureFlows.note: The managed domain extends domain controllers into selected regions so workloads use nearby highly available authentication endpoints.

security: Restrict delegated AD administration, protect trust credentials and use separate privileged accounts for domain management.
Permit only required AD ports between client, trust and DNS networks; avoid exposing domain controllers publicly.
Audit AD administrative events and monitor trust health while respecting the shared-responsibility boundary for managed controllers.
operations: Monitor DNS resolution, trust status, authentication latency and regional connectivity before investigating application-level failures.
Plan domain names, CIDR/subnet allocation and regions before creation because some domain properties are difficult or impossible to change.
Test hybrid failure modes, password/Kerberos time synchronization and domain-join recovery.
watchPoints: Managed Microsoft AD cannot simply join an existing forest as another managed domain; forest trusts connect separate forests.
DNS and firewall mistakes commonly appear as authentication or domain-join failures.
Google manages domain controllers, but customers still manage directory objects, group policy, trusts and application permissions.
cost: Pricing is based on managed domain/service tier and regional deployment; each region includes highly available domain controllers.
Hybrid networking, Cloud DNS, monitoring and domain-joined VMs have separate charges.
Adding regions improves locality/resilience but increases service cost.
alternatives: Managed Microsoft AD — Google-operated Microsoft AD domain services.
Self-managed AD on Compute Engine — full domain-controller and OS control.
Cloud Identity — workforce users, groups, devices and SaaS SSO.

comparisons.name: Managed Microsoft AD
comparisons.fit: Google-operated Microsoft AD domain services.

comparisons.name: Self-managed AD on Compute Engine
comparisons.fit: full domain-controller and OS control.

comparisons.name: Cloud Identity
comparisons.fit: workforce users, groups, devices and SaaS SSO.

memoryHooks: Two managed domain controllers per region provide zonal HA.
Trust connects forests; DNS and private network connectivity make the trust usable.
Exam clue: Windows domain join/Kerberos without managing DCs points to Managed Microsoft AD.

consoleSteps.detail: Set region, domain name, VPC peering, delegated admins and DNS.

consoleSteps.title: Apply security boundaries
consoleSteps.detail: Grant least-privilege administrative and runtime roles; configure network, encryption and audit controls appropriate to the service.

consoleSteps.detail: join a test VM, validate DNS/Kerberos and check domain-controller health.

services.summary: The API and Active Assist framework that analyzes resource configuration and usage to produce product-specific insights and actionable recommendations for cost, security, performance, reliability and manageability.
concepts: An insight describes an observed condition; a recommendation proposes operations that improve the resource. Both are scoped by project, location and type.
Recommendation state tracks workflow such as claimed, succeeded, failed or dismissed so automation and operators can coordinate without repeatedly applying advice.
Each recommender and insight type has its own IAM roles, refresh cadence, supported resources and evidence; recommendations are not universal policy.
applicationFit: Use Recommender to discover idle resources, rightsizing opportunities, IAM risks, reliability improvements and deprecation exposure.
Feed recommendations into reviewed automation where change risk is understood and rollback is available.
Use organization policy for mandatory guardrails and Monitoring alerts for live operational conditions.

architectureFlows.title: Human-reviewed optimization
architectureFlows.note: Active Assist produces evidence and proposed operations; an owner validates business context before applying and updating recommendation state.

architectureFlows.title: Automated recommendation pipeline
architectureFlows.note: The API exports selected recommendation types into a controlled workflow with risk checks, change execution and audit evidence.

security: Grant view and update permissions per recommender type; recommendations can expose sensitive resource, IAM and cost context.
Never auto-apply broad IAM, deletion or rightsizing recommendations without business-owner validation and rollback.
Use etags/state transitions to prevent concurrent or stale automation from applying the same recommendation.
operations: Inventory recommender and insight types relevant to the estate and record ownership and refresh expectations.
Track recommendation age, state, projected impact and post-change validation rather than counting open recommendations alone.
Use Cloud Audit Logs for recommendation access/state changes and the resource's own logs for applied changes.
watchPoints: Recommendations are advisory and can lack application context, seasonality or future demand.
A recommendation can become stale when resource state changes; refetch and use etag-aware updates.
Dismissing advice removes it from active workflow but does not create a mandatory exception policy.
cost: The Recommender API is generally not the dominant charge; savings or risk reduction relate to the underlying service.
Automation, exports, analytics and logging can add cost.
Projected savings are estimates and must be compared with performance, commitment and migration impact.
alternatives: Recommender — product-specific optimization insights and proposed actions.
Organization Policy — mandatory preventive constraints.
Cloud Monitoring — telemetry, SLOs and runtime alerting.

comparisons.name: Recommender
comparisons.fit: product-specific optimization insights and proposed actions.

comparisons.name: Organization Policy
comparisons.fit: mandatory preventive constraints.

comparisons.name: Cloud Monitoring
comparisons.fit: telemetry, SLOs and runtime alerting.

memoryHooks: Insight explains what was observed; recommendation explains what to change.
Recommendation state is workflow, not proof that the resource outcome succeeded.
Exam clue: rightsizing or IAM least-privilege advice from usage analysis points to Recommender.

consoleSteps.title: Open Recommender
consoleSteps.detail: Google Cloud Console → Recommender; select the intended scope and supported location.

consoleSteps.title: Configure the service
consoleSteps.detail: Set project/folder scope, recommender type, IAM and export/automation settings.

consoleSteps.title: Apply security boundaries
consoleSteps.detail: Grant least-privilege administrative and runtime roles; configure network, encryption and audit controls appropriate to the service.

consoleSteps.title: Validate operation
consoleSteps.detail: review insight evidence, claim/apply or dismiss a recommendation and verify outcome.

services.summary: An internal enterprise storefront where cloud administrators curate approved reference links, Terraform configurations, Deployment Manager templates and Marketplace products, then share catalogs to organization, folder or project audiences.
concepts: A catalog is a curated collection; a solution is an entry assigned to one or more catalogs. Users only discover catalogs shared to a resource they can access.

Solutions can be reference links, Terraform configurations, Deployment Manager templates or selected Cloud Marketplace products; the solution type determines whether Service Catalog only redirects or also deploys infrastructure.

Terraform solutions use Cloud Build to run Terraform and Cloud Storage for packaged modules and state-related artifacts; generated resources remain ordinary Google Cloud resources with their own IAM, lifecycle and charges.
applicationFit: Use Service Catalog to give platform teams a governed self-service front door for approved infrastructure patterns and enterprise resources.
Use separate catalogs and resource-level sharing when business units, environments or compliance zones need different approved offerings.
Do not use it as a public software marketplace, a CI/CD engine, a policy-enforcement substitute or a complete Terraform state-management platform.

architectureFlows.title: Curate and share an approved catalog
architectureFlows.note: A platform administrator publishes reviewed solutions once, assigns them to a catalog and exposes that catalog only to selected resource hierarchy audiences.

architectureFlows.title: Launch a Terraform solution
architectureFlows.note: The user supplies approved parameters; a controlled build identity reads the packaged module, executes Terraform and creates resources in the deployment project.

architectureFlows.title: Curated Marketplace adoption
architectureFlows.note: Administrators approve selected Marketplace software, publish it in an internal catalog and let eligible teams launch it under organizational controls.

consoleSteps.title: Enable and open Admin
consoleSteps.detail: Enable Service Catalog for the organization, select its administration project, then open Service Catalog Admin.

consoleSteps.title: Create the catalog
consoleSteps.detail: Create a named catalog; treat the immutable catalog name and administrative description as governed metadata.

consoleSteps.title: Create a solution
consoleSteps.detail: Choose link, Terraform, Deployment Manager or Marketplace; add owner, support and documentation details.

consoleSteps.title: Assign the solution
consoleSteps.detail: Attach the solution to the intended catalog. A solution is not discoverable merely because it exists.

consoleSteps.title: Share to an audience
consoleSteps.detail: Share the catalog to an organization, folder or project and grant only the required consumer visibility.

consoleSteps.title: Preview and launch
consoleSteps.detail: As a consumer, open Service Catalog, enter deployment parameters, preview changes and verify created resources.

security: Separate Catalog Admin, Catalog Manager and Catalog Consumer responsibilities; grant catalog producer roles to groups rather than broad project owners.
Treat the Cloud Build or user-managed service account as the deployment security boundary. It needs only the permissions required by the Terraform solution and access to the module bucket.
Catalog curation does not override Organization Policy, IAM or Deployment Manager constraints; use those controls to prevent a published solution from creating prohibited resources.
operations: Version solution packages and ownership metadata, test parameter schemas in a non-production project and publish changes through a review workflow.
Remove a solution from a catalog to stop new discovery without confusing that action with deletion of existing deployed resources.
Track Cloud Build executions, deployment failures, stale solution versions, support contacts and consumer adoption; validate deprovision behavior before production use.
watchPoints: Terraform modules must be packaged in the supported layout; modules in unsupported subdirectories can fail even when the Terraform code itself is valid.
Post-deployment resources and costs belong to the consumer project. Removing or updating the catalog entry does not automatically reconcile every existing deployment.

Deployment Manager solutions remain supported in the catalog, but Google recommends Terraform for an infrastructure-as-code approach; do not design new governance around a legacy template format by default.
cost: Service Catalog itself is free to use, but billing must be enabled because creating or launching solutions can consume chargeable services.
Terraform launches can incur Cloud Build, Cloud Storage, logging and networking charges in addition to every resource created by the module.
Model lifecycle cost—not only deployment cost—including idle infrastructure, software licensing, updates, support and deprovisioning.
alternatives: Service Catalog — internal discovery and governed launch of curated enterprise solutions.
Cloud Marketplace — public Google and partner product discovery, procurement and deployment.
Infrastructure Manager — managed Terraform deployment execution and lifecycle without an internal storefront.
Organization Policy — mandatory preventive constraints rather than a curated self-service experience.

comparisons.name: Service Catalog
comparisons.fit: Best fit for an internal, curated storefront shared to selected organization, folder or project audiences.

comparisons.name: Cloud Marketplace
comparisons.fit: Choose for Google and partner product procurement and public catalog discovery.

comparisons.name: Infrastructure Manager
comparisons.fit: Choose when managed Terraform deployment lifecycle is required without catalog curation.

memoryHooks: Solution is the item; catalog is the curated collection; sharing determines who can discover it.
Service Catalog governs discovery and launch—not the runtime behavior of resources created by a solution.
Exam clue: approved self-service blueprints for internal teams point to Service Catalog; mandatory denial rules point to Organization Policy.

services.summary: The Google Cloud infrastructure service that lists, enables and disables Google, Google Cloud and third-party APIs and services for consumer projects, with IAM-controlled state changes and long-running operations.
concepts: Most Google APIs must be enabled for a consumer project before credentials in that project can call them; enablement is project state, not permission to use every resource exposed by the API.
Service Usage represents services by names such as compute.googleapis.com and returns long-running operations for enable, disable and batch enable requests.
Service Usage Admin changes service state; Consumer can inspect state and consume quota/billing; Viewer provides read-only inspection. Product-specific IAM still authorizes actual API operations.
applicationFit: Use Service Usage in project bootstrapping, landing-zone automation and CI/CD prerequisites so required APIs are enabled deterministically.
Use inventory of enabled services for governance, attack-surface review and drift detection across projects.
Do not use Service Usage as an API gateway, API key store, runtime authorization layer or quota dashboard for every product.

architectureFlows.title: Project bootstrap and API enablement
architectureFlows.note: Provisioning automation enables required producer APIs first, waits for completion and only then creates resources through those APIs.

architectureFlows.title: Govern enabled-service drift
architectureFlows.note: A central inventory process lists enabled services, compares them with an approved baseline and routes exceptions to owners instead of disabling blindly.
architectureFlows.reference: Service Usage list and governance pattern

architectureFlows.title: Safe service disablement
architectureFlows.note: Operators assess dependencies and active resources before disablement because existing resources or dependent services can block or break the change.

consoleSteps.title: Select the consumer project
consoleSteps.detail: Open APIs & Services in the project that will consume the API; service enablement is scoped to that project.

consoleSteps.title: Open API Library
consoleSteps.detail: Search by the canonical service/API name and review prerequisites, terms, access approval and billing requirements.

consoleSteps.title: Enable the service
consoleSteps.detail: Choose Enable with a principal holding Service Usage Admin; wait for the operation to finish.

consoleSteps.title: Verify status
consoleSteps.detail: Open Enabled APIs & services or run gcloud services list --enabled and confirm the exact service name.

consoleSteps.title: Test product IAM
consoleSteps.detail: Call the API with the intended workload identity; enabling an API does not grant its product permissions.

consoleSteps.title: Disable cautiously
consoleSteps.detail: Check dependencies and active resources, schedule the change, disable, then verify state and audit evidence.

security: Restrict roles/serviceusage.serviceUsageAdmin because enabling a new API can expand a project's reachable control plane and disabling one can disrupt workloads.
Grant roles/serviceusage.serviceUsageConsumer to workload identities only when quota/billing consumption and service-state inspection are required; keep product roles separate.
Review Admin Activity audit logs for enable and disable operations and combine service inventory with organization policies where API availability must be centrally constrained.
operations: Declare required APIs in infrastructure code and wait for enablement operations before creating dependent resources to avoid eventual-consistency race failures.
Use batchEnable for project bootstrap, but account for write quotas and report the individual service that failed rather than retrying the whole build indefinitely.
Maintain an approved service baseline and dependency map; monitor unexpected enablement, failed operations and projects where critical APIs were disabled.
watchPoints: Enabling a service does not grant IAM permissions, create credentials, increase product quota or guarantee the API is available in every region.
Disabling an API can fail when resources still exist and can interrupt automation or applications that depend on it; assess dependencies before the change.
Service Usage API rate limits are separate from quotas of the service being enabled: default read calls are 240/minute and write calls are 60/minute; batchEnable counts as five write calls.
cost: Service Usage does not add a separate charge for toggling service state; charges come from the enabled APIs and the resources, requests, data and networking they consume.
An enabled but unused API is generally not itself a billable resource, but it can permit chargeable resources or requests to be created.
Include automation, inventory storage, audit-log routing and downstream product charges when evaluating governance cost.
alternatives: Service Usage — enable, disable and inspect API/service state for consumer projects.
Cloud Quotas — view and adjust quota preferences and limits for services.
API Gateway or Apigee — publish, secure and manage application APIs at runtime.
Organization Policy — centrally constrain resource behavior and supported service controls.

comparisons.name: Service Usage
comparisons.fit: Best fit for project-level API/service activation state and bootstrap automation.

comparisons.name: Cloud Quotas
comparisons.fit: Choose to inspect and manage allowed consumption after a service is available.

comparisons.name: API Gateway / Apigee
comparisons.fit: Choose to expose, authenticate, protect and observe application APIs.

memoryHooks: Enabled means the project may call the API; IAM decides who may do what; quota limits how much may be consumed.
Enable and disable return long-running operations—automation must wait for completion before assuming state changed.
Exam clue: gcloud services enable, APIs & Services Library or project bootstrap prerequisites point to Service Usage.
